analysis.one_liner: Raises Social Security benefits and pays for it with new taxes on high earners and investment income.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a committee vote or floor action in the 118th Congress; its last action was a House subcommittee referral in December 2024, and it died when the Congress ended on January 3, 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would boost Social Security checks across the board, use a cost-of-living formula that better matches what seniors actually buy, guarantee a minimum benefit near the poverty line for people who worked long careers at low wages, and let children of disabled or deceased workers keep benefits while in school until age 22. To pay for it, it would apply Social Security payroll taxes to wages above $250,000 (currently capped at $160,200 in 2023), raise the net investment income tax from 3.8% to 16.2%, and apply that investment tax to active business income for the first time. It would also merge the retirement and disability trust funds into one Social Security Trust Fund.
analysis.who_benefits: Current and future Social Security retirees and disability beneficiaries get a benefit increase (about a 5% first-tier boost plus a 22% adjustment to the bend point), a cost-of-living formula based on the Consumer Price Index for Elderly Consumers, and a new minimum benefit scaled to years worked that reaches about 125% of the poverty guideline for those with 30 or more years of work. Lifetime low earners, very old retirees whose benefits are recomputed, and full-time students up to 22 whose parent was retired, disabled, or deceased all gain directly.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Retirees, disability beneficiaries, low earners, students

how_it_helps.text: Raises the first bend point percentage from 90% to 95% and adds a 22% increase to the first bend point amount, raising benefits for current and future beneficiaries, with recomputation for people already on the rolls [S3].

Switches the annual cost-of-living adjustment to the Consumer Price Index for Elderly Consumers (CPI-E), which generally rises faster than the index now used because it weights medical and housing costs more heavily [S3].

Creates a new minimum benefit for lifetime low earners: a percentage of the poverty guideline based on years worked, from 6.25% at 11 years up to 125% at 30 or more years, with recomputation of benefits for people whose benefits were computed before November 2018 [S3].

Lets children of retired, disabled, or deceased workers stay on benefits as full-time students until age 22, instead of cutting off at 19, and makes the same change under the Railroad Retirement Act [S3].

Extends the Social Security payroll tax to wages and self-employment income above $250,000 (the 2023 cap was $160,200), and raises the net investment income tax from 3.8% to 16.2%, including on active trade or business income, with 62% of those investment-tax receipts flowing to the trust fund [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: High earners and high-income households. Wages and self-employment income above $250,000 would face the 12.4% combined Social Security payroll tax, which now stops at $160,200. Net investment income would be taxed at 16.2% instead of 3.8%, and for the first time active business income of owners of pass-through businesses would be subject to that tax. Under current law, benefits are calculated only on earnings up to the cap, so earnings above the cap would be taxed without adding proportionally to the taxpayer's own future benefit.
analysis.who_pays_short: High earners, investors, and business owners

drawbacks.text: The financing falls on a narrow base: the payroll tax above $250,000 would not increase the payer's own benefit, since the benefit formula counts earnings only up to the cap, so high earners would pay more into the system without a matching return [S3].

Raising the net investment income tax from 3.8% to 16.2% and extending it to active trade or business income substantially raises the effective tax rate on investment returns and on owners of pass-through businesses, who argue this falls on businesses that create jobs, not just on passive wealth [S3].

The CPI-E generally produces larger annual increases than the index now used, so the benefit side grows faster over time; critics would note this raises long-run program costs beyond what the new taxes might cover, and the bill provides no independent mechanism to balance the two [S2][S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit side is broad and concrete: larger checks for nearly every beneficiary, a poverty-floor minimum for career low earners, and a COLA that better tracks seniors' actual expenses. The cost is concentrated on the top: high earners, investors, and business owners, whose combined marginal tax rates on wages and investment income would rise sharply. The main honest concern is design rather than intent — the bill pairs faster-growing benefits with taxes that do not grow proportionally, leaving long-run balance to future Congresses — and the investment tax increase is steep enough that some business income is clearly caught in it. On balance the gains to typical beneficiaries are larger and more certain than the costs are to most households.

outcome.mechanism: The bill sat in committee for the entire two-year Congress — its only movement after the 2023 referral was a subcommittee referral in December 2024 — and expired without a markup, committee vote, or floor vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Janice Schakowsky introduced the Social Security Expansion Act on February 14, 2023 [S1][S5].
The House referred it to the Ways and Means Committee, and additionally to Education and the Workforce and Transportation and Infrastructure, on the day of introduction [S5].
The bill attracted 37 cosponsors, all Democrats [S4].
The only further action in the entire Congress was a referral to the Ways and Means Subcommittee on Social Security on December 17, 2024, two weeks before the Congress ended [S5].
No markup, committee vote, or floor vote ever occurred, and the bill expired on January 3, 2025, when the 118th Congress ended [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: High earners, investors, and owners of pass-through businesses are better off because the bill died: the payroll tax above $250,000 and the 16.2% investment income tax were never enacted, and existing tax treatment was preserved. Social Security beneficiaries gained nothing — no larger checks, no CPI-E cost-of-living formula, and no poverty-level minimum benefit.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: High earners and investors; beneficiaries gained nothing

for.name: Rep. Janice Schakowsky
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on February 14, 2023 and recruited 37 cosponsors for a benefits expansion paid for by taxes on high earners and investment income [S1][S4][S5].

for.name: 37 Democratic cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors, all from the Democratic Party, giving the bill a full party bloc of House support but no Republican cosponsor [S4].

against.name: Rep. Jason Smith
against.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: As chair of the committee with primary jurisdiction, never brought the bill to a markup or committee vote in the two-year Congress; the bill's only movement was a subcommittee referral in December 2024 [S5].

sides.party_line_note: Every cosponsor and the sponsor were Democrats — 37 of 37 — and no Republican supported the bill; with Republicans holding the House majority, it never advanced past referral [S4][S5].

industries.note: The bill taxes wages above $250,000 with the full 12.4% payroll tax and nearly quadruples the net investment income tax from 3.8% to 16.2%. That cost is the direct funding source for larger Social Security checks for ordinary beneficiaries [S3].

industries.industry: Owners of pass-through businesses (partnerships, S-corps, sole proprietors)
industries.note: For the first time, active trade or business income would be subject to the net investment income tax, which currently exempts it. This raises the tax bill of successful business owners specifically to fund benefits [S3].

industries.industry: Self-employed professionals above the earnings cap
industries.note: Self-employment earnings above $250,000 would face the Social Security self-employment tax, which now stops at $160,200; earnings above the cap would carry no proportional benefit accrual [S3].
